chapters.summary: Master the core agreement rule and the eight cases that decide your mark.

blocks.text: MODULE 1 · The Foundational Zero-to-Hero Grammar Engine Before any IELTS-specific technique, your sentences have to be mechanically sound. This module fixes the four faults that quietly lower your score on every single line of your writing and speaking: verbs that do not agree with their subjects, tenses that put events in the wrong time, missing or misused articles, and wrong prepositions. None of these is difficult. All of them are habits. Module 1 turns the correct habit into your default, so that by Module 2 you can build ambitious sentences on a base that does not leak marks. মডিউল ১-এর লক্ষ্য: ব্যান্ড ৬ পার হতে হলে আগে বাক্যের ভিত্তি নির্ভুল হতে হবে। এই মডিউল সেই চারটি মৌলিক ভু ল ঠিক করে যা প্রতিটি বাক্যে নম্বর কমায়: subject-verb agreement, tense, article, ও preposition।
Chapter 1 · Subject-Verb Agreement & Sentence Foundations
1.1 First, the building blocks (start here even if you think you know)

This book assumes you know nothing, so we begin with the parts of a sentence. You do not need to memorise these labels to speak Bangla, but almost every rule in this book is stated using them, so learn to recognise them. Every basic English sentence has two essential parts and often a third: • The subject is the person or thing the sentence is about, the one that does the action. In “Students study hard,” the subject is students.

• The verb is the action or the state of being. In “Students study hard,” the verb is study. The verb be (is, am, are, was, were) shows a state rather than an action: “The graph is clear.” • The object is the person or thing that receives the action. In “Students use the internet,” the object is the internet. The normal English order is Subject + Verb + Object (S + V + O). Students (S) use (V) the internet (O).

blocks.title: REGIONAL TIP (Bangla speakers)
blocks.text: REGIONAL TIP (Bangla speakers). Bangla is a Subject-Object-Verb language. আমি ভাত খাই is literally “I rice eat,” with the verb at the very end. English puts the verb second, right after the subject: “I eat rice.” When an English sentence you write feels wrong, the first thing to check is whether the verb has drifted to the end out of Bangla habit. “Agreement” simply means matching. Subject-verb agreement is the rule that the verb must match its subject in number. A singular subject (one) takes one form of the verb; a plural subject (more than one) takes another. That is the entire idea. The rest of this chapter is about the cases where spotting the true subject is tricky.
1.2 The core rule
In the present simple tense, the verb changes depending on whether the subject is singular or plural.

Subject Verb form Example Singular (he, she, it, one verb + s / es The student works hard. thing) Plural (they, more than one) base verb, no -s The students work hard. I / You / We / They base verb, no -s They work hard.

Notice the trap that catches thousands of Bangladeshi candidates: the -s is reversed between nouns and verbs. • On a noun, -s means plural: one student, many students. • On a verb, -s means singular: he works, they work. So a correct sentence often has an -s on either the noun or the verb, but not both: The student works. (singular noun, verb takes -s) The students work. (plural noun, verb has no -s)

blocks.text: 1.3 The cases that actually decide your mark

The core rule is easy. Marks are lost on the cases below, where the true subject is hidden, disguised, or further away from the verb than a nearer noun. Master these eight and you remove almost every agreement error from your writing.
Case 1 · Words between the subject and the verb

blocks.incorrect: The list of items are on the table.
The quality of the answers were poor.

blocks.text: The verb agrees with the true subject, never with the nearest noun. Writers are pulled toward the closest word, which is usually wrong. subject is “list” (singular), not “items”. Cross out the middle phrase and the truth is obvious: “The list … is.” Technique: find the subject, then mentally delete every word between it and the verb. “The list of items is.”
Case 2 · “The number of” versus “a number of”

This pair appears constantly in Writing Task 1, and the two behave in opposite ways. • “The number of + plural noun” takes a singular verb (the subject is number, one figure). • “A number of + plural noun” takes a plural verb (it simply means several). The number of tourists has increased since 2010. A number of tourists were waiting outside the museum.
Case 3 · Collective nouns

Words such as government, team, committee, family, company, public, staff name a group. In IELTS academic writing, treat each as a single unit and use a singular verb. The government is planning three new policies. The committee has reached a decision.

(British English sometimes allows a plural verb when the focus is on the individual members: “the team are arguing among themselves.” For IELTS academic Writing, stay singular and consistent. It is safer and never wrong.)
Case 4 · Indefinite pronouns are singular

Each, every, everyone, everybody, someone, anyone, nobody, either, neither, one are all singular, however plural the words around them look. Each of the students has a laptop. (not “have”) Everyone in the classes was present. Neither of the options is acceptable.
blocks.bn: each of, every, everyone সবসময় singular, পরে যত বড় বহুবচন noun-ই থাকু ক না কেন।

blocks.text: Case 5 · “Neither…nor,” “either…or,” “not only…but also”

With these paired connectors, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the one closest to the verb. Neither the manager nor the employees were informed. (nearer subject: employees, plural) Neither the employees nor the manager was informed. (nearer subject: manager, singular) Not only the students but also the teacher was worried.
Case 6 · Compound subjects joined by “and”

Two subjects joined by and are almost always plural. The teacher and the students were in the hall. Poverty and unemployment remain serious problems. Exception: when the two words describe a single combined thing, treat them as singular: “Bread and butter is a common breakfast.” This is rare in IELTS.
Case 7 · “There is” and “there are”

After there, the verb agrees with the real subject, which comes after the verb. There is a serious problem. (subject: problem, singular) There are several factors. (subject: factors, plural) There is a range of options. (subject: range, singular)
Case 8 · Uncountable nouns, amounts, and inverted structures

blocks.incorrect: The informations are correct and he gave many advices.

blocks.text: Uncountable nouns are treated as singular and never take a plural -s. Memorise the high- frequency IELTS set as a block: information, advice, knowledge, research, equipment, furniture, accommodation, traffic, progress, news, money, water, work correct and he gave a lot of advice. Amounts of time, money, and distance are treated as a single quantity, so they take a singular verb.

Ten years is a long time to wait. Five thousand taka is not enough. Inverted structures (where the verb comes before the subject) still agree with the subject. When a sentence begins with a negative adverb such as not only or hardly, find the subject after the verb and match it. Hardly ever does the government reverse such a decision. Only after 2010 did the figures begin to fall. (You will meet inversion in full in Chapter 8. Here, only notice that agreement still applies.)

blocks.title: Why Bangla speakers make agreement mistakes
blocks.body: Almost every subject-verb agreement error you make traces back to one fact: the Bangla verb does not change its ending to match a singular or plural subject the way the English verb does. Look at how Bangla behaves: Bangla Transliteration Literal meaning সে বাজারে যায় she bajare jay he / she goes to market তারা বাজারে যায় tara bajare jay they go to market The verb form যায় (jay) is identical for “he” and for “they.” Bangla marks person and formality, but it does not force the singular-plural switch on the verb that English demands. Because your first language never trained this switch, your ear does not warn you when it is missing. This produces the two most common Bangladeshi errors: Error type 1 · The dropped third-person -s. Because Bangla adds no -s, learners write the base verb everywhere. ✗ He go to the market every day. ✓ He goes to the market every day. ✗ The population increase rapidly. ✓ The population increases rapidly. Error type 2 · The dropped or wrong “is / are.” Bangla often has no separate word for is in a simple statement (সে ভালো = “he good,” with no “is”), so learners drop it or pick the wrong number. ✗ Many people is using the internet. / Many people using the internet. ✓ Many people are using the internet. ✗ The graph show that pollution have increased. ✓ The graph shows that pollution has increased. The fix is not “listen harder,” because your ear was never trained for this. The fix is a deliberate proofreading pass: after writing, go through every present-tense verb, find its true subject, and check the match on purpose. This is the “SVA” pass in the error-auditing routine you will build in Chapter 10.

blocks.title: Why this one rule caps your band
blocks.body: Subject-verb agreement is the error examiners notice first, because it appears in the very first line of almost every answer and it repeats. A script with recurring agreement errors cannot reach Band 7 in Grammatical Range and Accuracy, however good the ideas are, because the criterion at Band 7 requires that the majority of sentences are error-free. One agreement slip per sentence removes that. The damage is heaviest in Writing Task 1, which lives on subjects like the number of, the proportion of, the figure for, every one of which is singular and every one of which tempts you toward the plural noun beside it. IELTS in Action: Task 1: The number of visitors has risen sharply, whereas the proportion of local tourists has fallen. Task 2: Although the government provides free healthcare, demand continues to outstrip supply. Speaking Part 2: My family lives in a small town, and each of my brothers has a different job. Fixing agreement is the single highest-value, lowest-effort accuracy gain in the whole exam. It costs no new vocabulary and no new grammar. It costs only a habit.

chapters.title: Tense Mastery & Time Precision
chapters.summary: Put every verb in the right time. Five high-frequency tenses cover most IELTS Writing and Speaking.

blocks.text: 1. who works → who work: “who” refers to “people” (plural). 2. have increased → has increased: the subject is “the number” (singular). 3. There is many reasons → There are many reasons: the real subject “reasons” is plural. 4. technology allow → technology allows: “technology” is singular third person. 5. each of the major companies now offer → offers: “each of” is singular. 6. some managers believes → believe: “managers” is plural. 7. productivity fall → falls: “productivity” is singular (and uncountable).

8. staff is not → staff are not: here the focus is on the individual workers; plural reads better, and “are” is safe. (Singular “the staff is” is also defensible, but the following idea is about individual people not being present.) 9. the advantages … outweighs → outweigh: the subject is “advantages” (plural), not “work.” 10. this trend are → this trend is: “trend” is singular.

Chapter 2 · Tense Mastery & Time Precision
Subject-verb agreement made your verbs match. Tense makes them sit in the right time. In
IELTS this is not a small point of grammar; it is a matter of meaning. Writing Task 1 describes
data that already happened or is happening now, Task 2 predicts and generalises, and Speaking
moves constantly between past stories and future plans. Put a verb in the wrong time and you
have not just made a grammar slip, you have said something untrue about when it happened.
That is why examiners treat tense control as a core signal of the Band 6-to-7 jump.

blocks.text: 2.1 What a tense actually is (zero assumption)

An English tense carries two pieces of information at once: • Time: past, present, or future. (When did it happen?) • Aspect: simple, continuous, perfect, or perfect continuous. (Is it a whole finished event, an action in progress, an action linked to another time, or a mix?) Three times multiplied by four aspects gives the twelve tenses. That sounds like a lot, but the good news for IELTS is that five of them do about 90 per cent of the work, and this chapter foregrounds those five while still showing you the full map so nothing is a mystery. The four aspects, in plain words:

2.3 The five tenses IELTS actually rewards

You can describe any graph and answer any Speaking question accurately with these five. Master them before you worry about the rest. 1. Present simple for facts, habits, general truths, and Task 2 positions. 2. Present continuous for what is happening now and for current trends. 3. Past simple for finished events and historical graph data. 4. Present perfect for actions and trends that reach up to the present. 5. Future (will / going to) for predictions and plans. Two pairs inside this five cause almost all tense errors. The rest of the chapter drills those two pairs, because fixing them fixes most of your tense marks.
2.4 Critical pair 1 · Past simple versus present perfect

This is the single most common tense confusion for Bangladeshi candidates, and it is decisive in Task 1. • Use the past simple when the time is finished, and often stated: in 2010, last year, two decades ago, between 2000 and 2010. • Use the present perfect when the action reaches up to now, or when the exact time does not matter: signalled by since, for, over the past decade, recently, so far, already. Past simple: The population rose in 2010. (a finished year) Present perfect: The population has risen since 2010. (2010 up to the present) The clearest signal is the time word:

blocks.incorrect: The company has launched its first product in 2009.
Since 2020, remote work became far more common.

blocks.text: 2.5 Critical pair 2 · Present simple versus present continuous

• Use the present simple for a permanent fact, a habit, or a general truth. This is the tense of most Task 2 topic sentences and of process descriptions. • Use the present continuous for something happening right now or a temporary current trend, especially with words such as currently, at the moment, these days, nowadays. Present simple (general truth): Governments spend public money on healthcare. Present continuous (current trend): The number of remote workers is increasing steadily. The distinction matters in Task 1 when the data has no dates and is presented as a present situation, and in Task 2 introductions: Task 2 general truth: Many people believe that university education should be free. Task 1 current trend: Demand for electric vehicles is rising sharply at present.

blocks.text: 2.6 Future forms · will, going to, and the present continuous

Three forms cover the future in IELTS: • will + base verb: predictions, general future facts, and decisions made at the moment of speaking. > If this trend continues, sea levels will rise further. • be going to + base verb: plans already decided, and predictions based on present evidence. > The government is going to introduce a carbon tax next year. • present continuous: fixed personal arrangements (mostly Speaking). > I am meeting my supervisor tomorrow. For Task 1 projections (a graph that forecasts into the future) and Task 2 consequences, will is the workhorse: > Unless emissions are cut, the planet will face irreversible damage.
2.7 The perfect and continuous tenses you should at least recognise

You will not need all twelve constantly, but recognising them lets you read a prompt correctly and adds range when it is natural. • Past perfect (had + p.p.) shows which of two past events came first. Useful in Speaking Part 2 narratives. > By the time the report was published, the situation had already changed. • Present perfect continuous (have been + -ing) stresses the duration of a trend reaching now. > House prices have been rising steadily for over a decade. • Future perfect (will have + p.p.) projects a completed change by a future point, strong in Task 1 forecasts. > By 2040, the population will have doubled. Use these for genuine range, not decoration. One accurate past perfect in a Speaking narrative shows control; a forced one that does not fit reads as an error.

blocks.title: The continuous-tense trap
blocks.body: Two continuous-tense errors dominate Bangladeshi scripts. Both come from over-using the -ing form, partly because Bangla uses its continuous form more freely than English does. Error type 1 · Stative verbs cannot be continuous. Some verbs describe a state, not an action in progress: knowing, believing, wanting, and so on. English does not put these in the continuous form. This is the famous “I am knowing” error. Common stative verbs that must stay simple: know, believe, understand, mean, agree, want, need, prefer, like, love, hate, seem, appear, belong, own, contain, consist, depend, and have when it means possession. ✗ I am knowing the answer. / He is having two cars. ✓ I know the answer. / He has two cars. ✗ I am understanding your point now. ✓ I understand your point now. (Note: some of these verbs can be continuous when they change meaning to a real action. “He is having lunch” is correct because there have* means “eat,” an action, not possession. But know, believe, understand, want, need, belong, seem are never continuous.)*

blocks.title: Time frames win or lose Task 1
blocks.body: In Writing Task 1, tense is not optional accuracy; it is the backbone of the answer: • A chart with a past date range must stay in the past simple throughout. Slipping into the present here is a classic Band 5-to-6 marker. > Between 1990 and 2000, output rose steadily before it levelled off. • A trend that reaches the present takes the present perfect. > The demand for solar power has risen sharply over the past decade. • A graph with a future projection takes will or is expected to. > The figure is expected to reach 90 million by 2035. In Task 2, general truths and your own position sit in the present simple, while consequences and predictions take the future. Mixing these confuses your argument’s timeline, which examiners penalise under both Grammatical Range and Accuracy and Coherence. IELTS in Action: > Task 1: Car sales peaked in 2015, have fallen every year since, and are expected to stabilise after 2025. > Task 2: Because cities continue to expand, housing shortages will worsen unless governments act now. > Speaking Part 3: Attitudes have changed a great deal recently, and I think they will keep changing.

Chapter 3 · Articles (A, An, The) & Noun Types
If you fix only one chapter in this whole book, fix this one. Articles are the single highest-error
area for learners whose first language does not have them, and Bangla, Hindi, Urdu, and Nepali
all lack a direct equivalent of a / an / the. This is not a minor detail. Article errors are the
number one reason that otherwise strong Band 7 candidates stay stuck at Band 6.0,
because the mistakes are frequent, they appear in almost every sentence, and your ear cannot
catch them: your first language never trained it to.

The comforting news is that a small set of rules covers the great majority of cases, and articles
depend heavily on one prior idea, whether a noun is countable or uncountable, so we start
there.
অধ্যায় ৩-এর মূল কথা: article-ই সবচেয়ে বেশি ভু ল হওয়া বিষয়, কারণ বাংলায় a / an / the-এর সরাসরি কোনো রূপ
নেই। এই ভু লগুলোই ব্যান্ড ৬-এ আটকে রাখে। কান দিয়ে ধরা যায় না, তাই নিয়ম বুঝে সচেতনভাবে বসাতে হয়।

blocks.text: 3.1 First, countable versus uncountable nouns

Whether you can use a / an at all depends on this distinction, so learn it before the article rules. • Countable nouns can be counted and have a plural form: one book, two books; a student, five students. They can take a / an in the singular. • Uncountable nouns are treated as a single mass and have no plural form and no a / an: information (never informations), water, advice. The high-frequency uncountable nouns that trip up Bangladeshi candidates, worth memorising as a fixed block: information, advice, knowledge, research, equipment, furniture, accommodation, traffic, progress, news, money, water, work, luggage, baggage, software, staff, homework, feedback, transport, machinery, vocabulary To count an uncountable noun, use a partitive phrase (a unit word) plus of:

Wrong Right an advice a piece of advice an information a piece of information a research a study / a piece of research a furniture a piece of furniture / an item of furniture a luggage a piece of luggage
blocks.bn:
কিছু noun ইংরেজিতে uncountable, যদিও বাংলায় গোনা যায় বলে মনে হয়: information, advice, furniture,
equipment, research। এদের plural হয় না এবং a/an বসে না। গুনতে হলে a piece of advice, an item of
furniture বলতে হয়।

blocks.text: 3.2 The three articles and the zero article
There are three articles (a, an, the) and a fourth option, no article at all, called the zero article. Every singular countable noun needs one of these four decided on purpose.

a / an (the indefinite article) Use a / an for one, non-specific, singular, countable thing, usually mentioned for the first time. • The choice between a and an depends on sound, not spelling. Use an before a vowel sound, a before a consonant sound. > a university, a European country (these begin with a “y” consonant sound) > an hour, an honest man (silent h, so a vowel sound) > an MBA, an X-ray (letter names beginning with a vowel sound) I saw a documentary last night. (first mention, non-specific) She wants to become an engineer. (one, non-specific)

the (the definite article) Use the when the noun is specific: the reader or listener knows exactly which one you mean. That happens in several ways: • It was already mentioned: I saw a documentary. The documentary was about climate change. • There is only one of it: the sun, the government, the internet, the environment. • It is made specific by the words around it: the number of cars, the graph above, the capital of Bangladesh. • With superlatives and ordinals: the highest figure, the most important factor, the first step. The chart shows the number of visitors. (both specific) Solar power is the cleanest option available. (superlative)

the zero article (no article) Use no article for: • Plural countable nouns talked about in general: Books are expensive. Cars cause pollution. • Uncountable nouns talked about in general: Water is essential. Education matters. Poverty is rising. • Most proper nouns: names of most countries, cities, people, languages: Bangladesh, Dhaka, English. Education is a basic right. (general uncountable, zero article) Cars contribute to pollution. (general plural + general uncountable)
3.3 The decision process (use this when you proofread)
When you check any singular noun, run these questions in order: 1. Is it countable? If no (uncountable), you cannot use a / an. Choose the (if specific) or zero article (if general). Stop.
2. If yes (countable): is it specific, known, or unique? If yes, use the. 3. If it is not specific and singular: use a / an (by sound). 4. If it is a general plural: use the zero article.

(৩) নতুন ও একবচন হলে a/an, (৪) সাধারণ বহুবচন হলে কিছু ই না।

blocks.text: 3.4 Fixed cases worth memorising

Some article choices are just fixed and should be learned as items: • the internet, the environment, the economy, the government, the media, the public, the world take the (treated as unique). • Superlatives always take the: the best, the largest, the most significant. • Institutions used for their purpose take zero article: go to school, go to university, go to hospital (British usage), in prison, at home. Add the only when you mean the specific building: I went to the school to meet the head teacher. • Countries: most take zero article (Bangladesh, France, China), but a few plural or “united/republic” names take the: the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, the Philippines. • First mention then second mention: introduce with a, refer back with the. This is the classic a to the move examiners look for: > The chart shows a sharp rise in 2018. The rise continued into 2019.

blocks.title: Why Bangla speakers misuse articles
blocks.body: Because Bangla has no articles at all, the category does not exist in your mental grammar, so it must be learned as an English-only system rather than translated. Three error patterns dominate. Error type 1 · Omitting “the” for specific and unique things. ✗ Internet has changed our lives. / Government should fund school. ✓ The internet has changed our lives. / The government should fund schools. Why: “the internet” and “the government” are unique/specific; “schools” is a general plural. Error type 2 · Using “a / an” with uncountable nouns. This is the “an advice / an information” error. ✗ He gave me an advice. / She did a research on it. ✓ He gave me some advice / a piece of advice. / She did research / a study on it.
blocks.bn:
uncountable noun-এর আগে a/an বসে না। “an advice”, “an information”, “a research” ভু ল।
বলুন “a piece of advice”, “some information”, “a study”।

Error type 3 · Dropping the article entirely before a singular countable noun. Because
Bangla can say “government should take step” with no article at all, learners carry that over.
     ✗ Government should take step to reduce pollution. ✓ The government should take
     steps to reduce pollution. Why: “the government” needs the definite article, and “step”
     must be plural here (general steps).
The fix, once again, is a deliberate article pass when you proofread: go to every singular
countable noun and ask the four questions in 3.3. Do not rely on your ear.

blocks.title: The number one Band 6 ceiling
blocks.body: Article control is audited densely across every task. In Task 1 a single sentence can require three separate article decisions: “The chart shows the number of visitors to a museum.” In Task 2 generalisations, the pattern flips to zero article and the: “Governments should protect the environment.” Because the errors are so frequent, they are the classic thing separating a script that reads like Band 7 in ideas but scores Band 6 in Grammatical Range and Accuracy. Examiners do not need many article slips to conclude that accuracy is inconsistent. Conversely, consistent article control is one of the clearest Band 6.5-plus signals you can send. IELTS in Action: > Task 1: The graph illustrates the proportion of households with an internet connection. (the, the, an) > Task 2: Education is widely seen as the key to development, and governments should therefore fund schools properly. (zero, the, zero, zero, zero) > Speaking Part 2: The person who influenced me most was a teacher at my primary school.

Chapter 4 · Prepositions & Dependency Rules
Prepositions are the small words (in, on, at, by, for, to, of, from, with) that show how other
words relate in time, place, and direction. They look trivial, but they carry a large share of the
errors on this test, for one reason: prepositions are memorised by pattern, not by logic.
There is no rule that explains why English says interested in but good at and afraid of. These
are fixed collocations, and they either sound right to a native ear or they do not.
For a Bangla speaker, that is a problem, because your instinct is to translate the Bangla
preposition directly, and Bangla maps its relationships differently. This chapter does two
things: it gives you the high-frequency patterns to memorise as blocks, and it targets the
specific direct-translation errors that mark a script as Bangladeshi.
অধ্যায় ৪-এর মূল কথা: preposition যুক্তি দিয়ে নয়, প্যাটার্ন মুখস্থ করে শিখতে হয়। বাংলা থেকে সরাসরি অনুবাদ করলে ভু ল
হয় (যেমন “discuss about”, “according to me”)। এই অধ্যায় সেই fixed collocation আর অনুবাদজনিত
ভু লগুলো ঠিক করে।

blocks.text: 4.1 What a preposition does (zero assumption)

A preposition sits before a noun or pronoun and shows a relationship: the book is on the table (place), the meeting is at three (time), she walked into the room (direction). The noun after it is called its object. One key rule you already met in the tenses chapter returns here: after a preposition, a verb always takes the -ing form, never the infinitive. Interested in studying, responsible for managing, capable of solving.
4.2 Prepositions of time · in, on, at, and their neighbours
The three core time prepositions follow a “zooming in” logic, from long periods to exact points.

Preposition Used with Examples in months, years, seasons, in July, in 2020, in winter, in centuries, long periods the 1990s on days and dates on Monday, on 5 May, on weekdays at clock times and fixed points at 5 p.m., at night, at the weekend, at the start

Other time prepositions that matter for IELTS: • since + a starting point (goes with the present perfect): since 2010, since January. • for + a length of time: for five years, for a decade. • during + a period (when something happens within it): during the 1990s, during the recession. • by + a deadline (not later than): by 2030, by the end of the decade.

blocks.incorrect: In Monday the shop is closed. / The population grew since five years.

blocks.text: • from … to / until + a span: from 2000 to 2010, until 2015. the shop is closed. / The population grew for five years.
4.3 Prepositions of place and direction

• in = inside a space or area: in the room, in Dhaka, in the world. • on = on a surface or line: on the wall, on the coast, on the second floor. • at = at a specific point or place: at the station, at the top, at home. • into / onto / to show movement or direction: walk into the room, climb onto the roof, go to work. The figures are shown in the chart, on the vertical axis, at the top of the page.
4.4 The Task 1 data prepositions (memorise as fixed phrases)
These combinations describe movement and quantity on a graph. They are non-negotiable in Writing Task 1, and examiners expect every one of them to be exact.

blocks.incorrect: Sales increased with 20 per cent and reached to a peak in June.

blocks.text: Phrase Use Example increase / rise by the size of a change rose by 10 per cent from X to Y start and end points grew from 10 to 20 million a rise / an increase of after the noun form an increase of 10 per cent reach a peak / stand at a specific value peaked at 40 per cent fall / drop to the destination value fell to a low of 5 between X and Y a range or a time span between 2000 and 2010 20 per cent and reached a peak in June. Why: “increase by” a percentage; “reach a peak” takes no preposition after “reach.” A single strong Task 1 sentence often chains several of these: > The price rose by five dollars, from 20 to 25, reaching a peak of 25 in March.

blocks.text: 4.5 Dependent prepositions (the ones after specific words)

Many verbs, adjectives, and nouns are followed by a fixed preposition. There is no logic; you learn each as a unit. Below are the highest-frequency IELTS collocations. Memorise them in blocks and use them until they feel automatic. Verb + preposition

Collocation Example depend on The outcome depends on funding. lead to Industrialisation leads to pollution. result in The policy resulted in higher costs. result from The damage resulted from neglect. contribute to Cars contribute to air pollution. consist of The panel consists of five experts. deal with Governments must deal with poverty. focus on The essay focuses on two causes. rely on Rural areas rely on agriculture. suffer from Many cities suffer from congestion. benefit from Students benefit from feedback. apply for She applied for a scholarship. participate in Few citizens participate in elections. invest in Governments should invest in transport. cope with Families struggle to cope with rising costs.

Collocation Example an increase / rise in an increase in demand a reason for the main reason for this a solution to a solution to the problem
Collocation Example an effect / impact on the effect on health a demand for growing demand for housing a lack of a lack of funding the cause of the cause of the decline

blocks.title: Small words, real marks
blocks.body: Prepositions affect your score in two visible places. In Writing Task 1, the data prepositions (by, from, to, of, at) are so standard that getting one wrong stands out immediately as an accuracy error. In Writing Task 2 and Speaking, the dependent prepositions (depend on, lead to, responsible for, solution to) and the direct-translation errors (discuss about, according to me) are the ones that separate controlled from uncontrolled English. Because these are collocations, correct ones also lift your Lexical Resource score, so the payoff is double. MODULE 2 · Band 7.0+ Complex Structures & Range Booster
Module 1 made your sentences correct. Module 2 makes them varied. This is the stage where
scripts stop sounding like a list of short, safe statements and start reading like connected
argument. The Band 7 descriptor for Grammatical Range and Accuracy asks for “a variety of
complex structures used with some flexibility,” and this module supplies exactly that: complex
sentences built from subordinate clauses, the passive voice for academic tone, and conditionals
for arguing about possibilities. Range and accuracy must grow together, so keep applying the
Module 1 proofreading habits to every ambitious sentence you now build.

Chapter 5 · Complex Sentences & Subordinate Clauses
The complex sentence is the single most important structure for reaching Band 7, because it is
the clearest signal of range. It lets you show a logical relationship between two ideas (contrast,
reason, condition, time) inside one controlled sentence, instead of two short disconnected ones.
Master this chapter and your writing stops sounding like a beginner’s list.
অধ্যায় ৫-এর মূল কথা: complex sentence-ই ব্যান্ড ৭-এ পৌঁছানোর সবচেয়ে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ কাঠামো, কারণ এটি range দেখায়
এবং দুটি ধারণার মধ্যে যুক্তিসম্পর্ক (বৈপরীত্য, কারণ, শর্ত, সময়) একটি বাক্যে বাঁধে।

blocks.text: 5.1 Clause basics (start here)

A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb. There are two kinds, and the whole chapter rests on telling them apart. • An independent clause expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence: “Cities offer jobs.” • A dependent (subordinate) clause has a subject and a verb but cannot stand alone, because a subordinating word at its front leaves it unfinished: “Although cities offer jobs …” This makes you wait for the rest. A complex sentence joins one independent clause with at least one dependent clause: Although cities offer jobs, (dependent) they are crowded. (independent)
5.2 The three sentence types, and why complex wins marks
You met the first two in Chapter 1. Here is the full set:

Type Structure Example Simple one independent clause Cities offer jobs. Compound two independent clauses + Cities offer jobs, but they are FANBOYS crowded. Complex independent + dependent Although cities offer jobs, clause they are crowded.

A Band 5 script is mostly simple sentences. A Band 6 script mixes simple and compound. A Band 7 script controls complex sentences and uses a variety of them. That is the jump this chapter delivers. There are two main tools: adverbial clauses (5.3) and relative clauses (5.4).
5.3 Adverbial (subordinate) clauses

An adverbial clause is a dependent clause that begins with a subordinating conjunction and shows how its idea relates to the main clause. Learn the subordinators grouped by the relationship they signal.

Relationship Subordinators Example Contrast although, even though, Although it is costly, it whereas, while works. Reason because, since, as Prices rose because demand outstripped supply. Condition if, unless, provided that, as Unless action is taken, the long as trend will continue. Time when, after, before, once, Once fees rose, enrolment while dropped. Purpose so that, in order that Laws were tightened so that accidents would fall. Result so … that, such … that The cost was so high that the plan collapsed.

For purpose, the most useful compact form is in order to + base verb (or simply to + base verb): > The city expanded the metro in order to reduce congestion. The comma rule (memorise this). If the dependent clause comes first, put a comma after it. If it comes second, usually use no comma. Although it is costly, it works. (fronted dependent clause, comma) It works although it is costly. (dependent clause second, no comma)

dependent clause আগে বসলে পরে কমা দিন (Although it is costly, it works); পরে বসলে সাধারণত কমা
লাগে না (It works although it is costly)।

blocks.text: 5.4 Relative clauses

A relative clause adds information about a noun using a relative pronoun: who, which, that, where, whose. It lets you fold what would be two short sentences into one mature sentence, which directly serves range.

Pronoun Refers to Example who people Students who study abroad gain independence. which things Solar power, which is clean, is expanding. that people or things (defining The policy that failed was only) expensive. where places Cities where rents are high lose young workers. whose possession Families whose income is low need support.

blocks.incorrect: My school, that is very old, is famous. >
People which live in cities they pay more rent. >

blocks.text: Defining versus non-defining: the comma changes the meaning This is the part that carries the marks, and it is not decorative. The commas change what the sentence means. • A defining clause identifies which one and is essential. It takes no commas. > Students who cheat are expelled. (only the cheating ones) • A non-defining clause adds extra, non-essential information and is fenced with commas on both sides. > The students, who were tired, left early. (all of them, and by the way they were tired) Two rules follow from this: 1. Use that only in defining clauses. In non-defining clauses use which or who, never that. > famous. 2. Do not repeat the subject with a pronoun after the relative clause. This is a very common Bangladeshi error. > People who live in cities pay more rent.

defining clause-এ; non-defining-এ which/who. এবং relative clause-এর পরে আবার they/it দিয়ে

Reduced relative clauses (a Band 8 touch)
You can often drop the relative pronoun and the verb be to make a tighter phrase. You will
meet this fully as participial phrases in Chapter 8; notice it here. > Governments that invest in
renewables … → Governments investing in renewables … > The report which was published
last year … → The report published last year …

blocks.title: Fragments, run-ons, and comma splices
blocks.body: When learners first attempt complex sentences, three punctuation faults appear. All three come from not yet feeling where one clause ends and the next begins. Fault 1 · The fragment (a dependent clause left alone). A dependent clause is not a sentence. Attaching a full stop after it does not make it one. > ✗ Because the weather was bad. The event was cancelled. > ✓ Because the weather was bad, the event was cancelled. > ✗ Even though the policy was popular. > ✓ Even though the policy was popular, it was withdrawn. Fault 2 · The run-on (two clauses with no join). Two independent clauses cannot simply be pushed together. > ✗ I studied hard I failed the exam. > ✓ I studied hard, but I failed the exam. Fault 3 · The comma splice (two clauses joined by only a comma). This is the most common of the three. > ✗ Internet use rose rapidly, people spent more time online. > ✓ Internet use rose rapidly, so people spent more time online. (comma + FANBOYS) > ✓ Internet use rose rapidly; consequently, people spent more time online. (semicolon) > ✓ As internet use rose rapidly, people spent more time online. (make one clause dependent) The four legal ways to join two independent clauses: a full stop, a semicolon, a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS), or by turning one clause into a dependent clause with a subordinator. A lone comma is never one of them.

blocks.title: The Band 7 range requirement
blocks.body: The phrase in the official Band 7 descriptor is “a variety of complex structures.” That word variety matters: an essay that uses only because clauses does not show range, even if every one is correct. Aim to deploy a spread across a Task 2 essay: a contrast clause (although), a reason clause (since), a conditional (if), and a relative clause or two. In Task 2, arguments are literally built from contrast and reason clauses; in Speaking Part 3, abstract answers gain range the same way. IELTS in Action: > Task 2 (contrast + relative): While online learning widens access, it cannot fully replace the discipline that a classroom provides. > Task 2 (reason + condition): Because demand continues to rise, prices will keep climbing unless supply increases. > Speaking Part 3: People who grow up in cities often value convenience, whereas those from rural areas tend to prioritise community.

Chapter 6 · Passive Voice & Academic Detachment
The passive voice turns the object of an action into the subject of the sentence, so the focus falls
on what happens rather than who does it. It is one of the two or three structures that give
academic writing its formal, impersonal tone, and it is essential in two specific IELTS places:

the Task 1 process diagram, which is written almost entirely in the passive, and the Task 2
essay, where an impersonal register sounds more objective than a personal one. Used well, the
passive lifts your tone; used everywhere, it makes writing heavy and evasive. This chapter
teaches both the form and the judgement.
অধ্যায় ৬-এর মূল কথা: passive voice-এ কাজের object বাক্যের subject হয়, ফোকাস পড়ে “কী ঘটল” তার উপর, “কে
করল” তার উপর নয়। Task 1 process diagram প্রায় পুরোটাই passive, আর Task 2-তে passive নৈর্ব্যক্তিক
academic সুর দেয়। তবে অতিরিক্ত ব্যবহার লেখাকে ভারী করে ফেলে।

blocks.text: 6.1 What the passive is (zero assumption)

Compare two sentences that describe the same event: Active: Workers transport the materials. (subject = workers, the doer) Passive: The materials are transported (by workers). (subject = materials, the receiver) In the active voice, the subject does the action. In the passive voice, the subject receives the action, and the doer either disappears or is added at the end with by. The formula never changes: Object of the active sentence + a form of be + past participle (+ by + doer) The two moving parts are the correct form of be (which carries the tense) and the past participle (the third form of the verb: transport / transported / transported; build / built / built; write / wrote / written). Get those two right and the passive is right.
6.2 The passive across the tenses
The tense lives in the be part; the past participle stays the same. This table shows the transformation for the tenses you actually need.

Tense Active Passive Present simple Workers transport the goods. The goods are transported. Present continuous Workers are transporting the The goods are being goods. transported. Past simple Workers transported the The goods were goods. transported. Past continuous Workers were transporting The goods were being the goods. transported. Present perfect Workers have transported The goods have been the goods. transported. Past perfect Workers had transported the The goods had been goods. transported.
Tense Active Passive Future (will) Workers will transport the The goods will be goods. transported. Modal Workers should transport The goods should be the goods. transported.
Notice the pattern: whatever the tense, you always end with the past participle (transported), and the be form in front of it changes to carry the time.

blocks.text: 6.3 When to choose the passive

The passive is a tool for specific situations, not a default. Use it when: • The doer is unknown, obvious, or unimportant. “The bottles are washed” is better than naming who washes them, because it does not matter. > New traffic laws were introduced in 2019. (who introduced them is obvious: the authorities.) • You want an objective, impersonal tone. This is the register Task 2 rewards. > It is widely believed that education reduces poverty. (more academic than “Many people believe …”) • You are describing a process. Every step of a manufacturing or natural process is naturally passive, because the focus is on the stages, not on who performs them. > First, the raw beans are harvested. They are then dried, roasted, and ground before the coffee is packaged.
6.4 Academic detachment: the impersonal “It is …” structures
A specific, high-value use of the passive is to remove “I” and “people” from a general claim, which sounds more objective. Learn these frames:

Personal (weaker) Impersonal (more academic) Many people think that … It is thought that … People often argue that … It is often argued that … Everyone knows that … It is widely known that … People say that tourism harms the coast. It is said that tourism harms the coast. We can clearly see that … It can be seen that … Personal: People say that tourism harms the coast. Impersonal: It is said that tourism harms the coast. These are especially useful for the introduction and topic sentences of a Task 2 essay, where you want to present a general view without claiming it as your own.

blocks.title: Where the passive earns marks
blocks.body: Writing Task 1 process diagrams are the clearest case: because the doer of each step is irrelevant, the whole description runs in the passive present simple. A process answer that stays in the active (“Someone harvests the beans, then someone dries them”) sounds wrong and childish; the passive is expected. Writing Task 2 uses the passive more selectively, for the impersonal tone of general statements and for describing effects where the cause is general. Combined with the active for your own arguments, it shows the examiner you can control register, which supports both Grammatical Range and Accuracy and the tone side of the task. IELTS in Action: > Task 1 process: Once the cocoa pods have been harvested, the beans are removed, fermented, and left to dry in the sun. > Task 2 impersonal: It is often argued that stricter regulation is needed, although the costs are frequently underestimated. > Speaking Part 3: A lot is being done to improve recycling, but more could be achieved with better public awareness.

Chapter 7 · Conditionals, Hedging & Hypothetical Reasoning
Conditionals let you argue about situations that may or may not be real: if this happens, that
will follow. They are the natural grammar of cause and effect, which is why Writing Task 2 and
Speaking Part 3 depend on them so heavily. Alongside conditionals sits a second, closely related
skill: hedging, the art of making a claim cautiously rather than absolutely. Together they let

you reason about possibilities with the measured, academic tone that separates a Band 8
argument from a Band 6 one. A Band 6 writer says “This will destroy society.” A Band 8 writer
says “This could, in some cases, undermine social cohesion.” Same idea, very different control.
অধ্যায় ৭-এর মূল কথা: conditional দিয়ে সম্ভাব্য বা কাল্পনিক পরিস্থিতি নিয়ে যুক্তি দেওয়া যায় (if…, then…)। আর
hedging মানে দাবিকে চরমভাবে না বলে সতর্ক ভাবে বলা। দুটো মিলে Task 2 ও Speaking Part 3-এর cause-and-
effect যুক্তিকে academic সুর দেয়।

blocks.text: 7.1 What a conditional is (zero assumption)

A conditional sentence has two parts: • the if-clause (the condition): If fees rise … • the result clause (the consequence): … fewer students will enrol. Either part can come first. When the if-clause comes first, put a comma after it. When the result comes first, no comma is needed. If fees rise, fewer students will enrol. (if-clause first, comma) Fewer students will enrol if fees rise. (result first, no comma) The only thing that changes between the different conditionals is the verb forms in each half. Get those matched and the conditional is correct.
7.2 The five conditionals
IELTS needs the first three reliably, plus recognition of the third and mixed for a high band.

Type Form Use Example Zero If + present, present a general truth or If you heat ice, it scientific fact melts. First If + present, will + a real, likely future If fees rise, fewer base possibility students will enrol. Second If + past, would + a hypothetical or If governments base unlikely invested more, present/future pollution would fall. Third If + had + p.p., a past situation that If she had studied, would have + p.p. did not happen she would have passed. Mixed If + had + p.p., a past condition with If I had saved would + base (now) a present result money, I would be wealthy now.

Read the second conditional carefully. Its if-clause looks like the past (if governments invested), but it talks about an imaginary present or future, not a past event. Read it as “supposing this were true,” not as a past story. The formal “were”. In the second conditional, formal English uses were for all subjects, including I, he, she, it: > If I were the prime minister, I would reform the tax system. > If public transport were free, more people would use it.

blocks.text: 7.3 The error that decides the mark: do not mix the halves

blocks.incorrect: If governments would invest more, pollution will decrease.

blocks.text: Each conditional keeps its two halves matched. The most common mistake is putting will or would in the if-clause, or mixing a first-conditional half with a second-conditional half. invested more, pollution would decrease. (clean second conditional.) will recycle more, waste would decrease. decrease. (clean first conditional.) The rule to memorise: never put “will” or “would” directly after “if.” The if-clause takes the present (first/zero), the past (second), or the past perfect (third); the will/would belongs in the result clause only.

blocks.text: 7.4 Modals of possibility and academic hedging

Hedging means qualifying a claim so it is not absolute. Band 8 and 9 writing rarely says X will definitely solve Y; it says X could help to reduce Y. This is not weakness. It is a mark of academic maturity, because careful writers know that few things in the real world are certain. IELTS examiners reward it directly. Your hedging toolkit:

Tool Examples Sample use Modals may, might, could, would Fees may discourage some students. Lexical verbs tend to, appear to, seem to Prices tend to rise in winter. Adverbs often, generally, frequently, This is, to some extent, a in many cases, to some matter of policy. extent, arguably

Tool Examples Sample use Quantity words many, most, a significant Most experts agree, rather number of than “everyone.” Full phrases it is arguable that, it could be It could be argued that argued that, there is a stricter laws are needed. tendency for, X is likely to

Two everyday upgrades to build the habit: Absolute: Rising fees will reduce enrolment. → Hedged: Rising fees may reduce enrolment. Absolute: Technology destroys traditional jobs. → Hedged: Technology tends to displace some traditional jobs.

cases, it could be argued that ব্যবহার করুন। এটা দুর্বলতা নয়, academic পরিপক্বতার চিহ্ন।

blocks.body: A recurring feature of Bangladeshi (and generally lower-band) Task 2 writing is the absolute, over-generalised claim: “Everyone will be destroyed,” “It always happens,” “All students are lazy.” These hurt you twice: they read as unacademic (no careful thinker claims total certainty), and they are easy to attack, which weakens your argument. blocks.title: Conditionals and hedging in the exam
blocks.body: Second conditionals are the natural grammar of Task 2 solution paragraphs and Speaking Part 3 speculation, where you argue about hypotheticals: If public transport were free, fewer people would drive. First conditionals carry real consequences in problem-and-solution essays: If emissions are not cut, the planet will face serious harm. Hedging runs through the whole of Task 2 and Speaking Part 3. It protects every generalisation you make, and it is one of the clearest signals of the careful, qualified reasoning that Band 7 and above require. A script full of absolute claims is capped, however strong its grammar, because the reasoning sounds immature. IELTS in Action: > Task 2 (first conditional): If governments fail to invest in flood defences, coastal cities will become increasingly vulnerable. > Task 2 (second + hedge): If education were genuinely free, participation would probably rise, although the effect might vary between regions. > Speaking Part 3: If I were in charge of the city, I would prioritise public transport, because it tends to benefit the most people.

MODULE 3 · Band 9.0 Masterclass (Advanced Linguistic Precision)
Modules 1 and 2 gave you accuracy and range: correct sentences, and a variety of complex ones.
That is enough for Band 7. Module 3 adds the structures that push a script from Band 7 up
towards Band 8.5 and 9.0: the rare, sophisticated forms that appear naturally in the writing of
highly proficient users. There are only two chapters here, because at this level a little goes a
long way. Inversion and cleft sentences (Chapter 8) create emphasis; nominalisation
(Chapter 9) creates academic density. Both must be used sparingly and accurately. One well-
placed inverted sentence signals control; three forced ones signal a candidate showing off.
Precision, not quantity, is the Band 9 habit.

Chapter 8 · Inversion, Cleft Sentences & Advanced Emphasis
Standard English puts the subject before the verb. Emphasis grammar deliberately breaks
that order, or restructures the sentence, to throw weight onto one idea. Examiners recognise

these structures instantly as markers of a very high band, precisely because most candidates
never attempt them, and the ones who do often get them wrong. This chapter gives you two
reliable tools: inversion and cleft sentences. Learn a small number of fixed patterns, use each
occasionally, and get it exactly right.
অধ্যায় ৮-এর মূল কথা: সাধারণ ইংরেজিতে subject আগে, verb পরে। emphasis grammar ইচ্ছা করে সেই ক্রম ভাঙে
বা বাক্য পুনর্গঠন করে কোনো একটি ধারণায় জোর দেয়। inversion ও cleft, এই দুটি টু ল অল্প কিন্তু নির্ভুলভাবে ব্যবহার
করলে খুব উঁচু ব্যান্ডের সংকেত দেয়।

blocks.text: 8.1 Negative inversion

When a sentence begins with a negative or limiting adverbial (a word or phrase meaning “not,” “rarely,” “only,” “never”), English inverts the subject and the auxiliary verb, exactly as in a question. This is the most useful inversion pattern for IELTS. The form: negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + main verb. The common triggers, with model sentences:

Trigger Inverted example Not only … but also Not only has the internet changed communication, but it has also transformed work. Never (before) Never before have governments faced such a challenge. Rarely / Seldom Rarely does a single policy satisfy everyone. Hardly ever Hardly ever does the government reverse such a decision. Little Little did people realise how quickly the situation would change. No sooner … than No sooner had the law passed than protests began. Not until … Not until recently did the public grasp the danger. Only after / Only when / Only then Only after the crisis did the government act. Under no circumstances Under no circumstances should safety be compromised.

Two mechanical points that learners miss: 1. If there is no auxiliary in the plain sentence, add do / does / did (just as you do to form a question). “A policy rarely satisfies everyone” becomes “Rarely does a policy satisfy everyone” (the -s moves onto does, and the main verb returns to its base form satisfy).

blocks.incorrect: Not only the internet has changed communication, but also work.

blocks.text: 2. Only the subject and auxiliary swap, not the whole sentence. The rest of the clause keeps its normal order. the internet changed communication, but it has also changed work.

under no circumstances) থাকলে subject ও auxiliary উল্টে যায়, প্রশ্নের মতো। auxiliary না থাকলে

everyone.”

blocks.text: 8.2 Fronting (emphasis without full inversion)

A gentler form of emphasis is fronting: moving a phrase to the start of the sentence for weight, without necessarily inverting subject and verb. It is lower risk than inversion and still adds variety. Normal: Urban centres offer better healthcare compared to rural areas. Fronted: Compared to rural areas, urban centres offer better healthcare. Normal: Air quality barely improved despite the scheme. Fronted: Despite the scheme, air quality barely improved. Fronting is safe, natural, and useful when you simply want to vary how sentences open across a paragraph.
8.3 Cleft sentences
A cleft sentence splits one idea into two parts to spotlight the important element. The name comes from “cleave,” to split. Two patterns matter for IELTS.

The it-cleft: It is / was X that … Use it to spotlight a noun, a person, or a time. Plain: Education drives development. Cleft: It is education that drives development. (spotlight: education.) Plain: The crisis began in 2008. Cleft: It was in 2008 that the crisis began. (spotlight: the time.)

The what-cleft: What … is … Use it to spotlight an action or a need, especially in Task 2 solution sentences. Plain: We need stronger regulation. Cleft: What is needed is stronger regulation. Plain: The city lacks affordable housing. Cleft: What the city lacks is affordable housing. Two other useful cleft frames:

• The reason (why) … is that …: The reason many students struggle is that they memorise rather than practise. • All (that) … is …: All that is required is a small change in behaviour. Agreement note: the linking verb in a what-cleft is usually singular (What is needed is …), even before a plural noun, because what is treated as singular.

blocks.title: The Band 8.5 to 9.0 signal
blocks.body: The Band 9 descriptor asks for “a wide range of structures used naturally, appropriately, and with full flexibility.” Inversion and cleft sentences are among the rarest of those structures, so a single accurate example, placed where it genuinely adds emphasis, tells the examiner you operate at the top of the scale. They fit most naturally in the conclusion or the key argument of a Task 2 essay, and in Speaking Part 3, where a well-timed “What really matters is …” sounds both fluent and controlled. IELTS in Action: > Task 2 (inversion): Not only does renewable energy reduce emissions, but it also creates long-term employment. > Task 2 (what-cleft): What is ultimately required is a shift in public attitudes, not merely new legislation. > Speaking Part 3 (it-cleft): It is often the youngest generation that adapts most quickly to technological change.

Chapter 9 · Nominalisation & Academic Density
Nominalisation is the habit of turning a verb or an adjective into a noun, and then building
the sentence around that noun. “The population increased rapidly” becomes “There was a rapid
increase in the population,” and “Education is important” becomes “the importance of
education.” It sounds like a small move, but it is one of the clearest markers of native-level
academic writing, because it makes a sentence denser, more formal, and more objective. It is
also the engine of paraphrasing, which is why it matters so much in Task 1. This is the last new
structure in the book, and, like inversion, it works best in moderation.

অধ্যায় ৯-এর মূল কথা: nominalisation মানে verb বা adjective-কে noun-এ রূপান্তর করে সেই noun-কে ঘিরে
বাক্য গড়া। “The population increased” → “an increase in the population”; “Education is
important” → “the importance of education”। এটি লেখাকে ঘন, আনুষ্ঠানিক ও নৈর্ব্যক্তিক করে এবং
paraphrasing-এর মূল হাতিয়ার।

blocks.text: 9.1 What nominalisation is (zero assumption)

Every action verb and most descriptive adjectives have a noun form in the same word family. Nominalisation uses that noun form as the main idea of the sentence, instead of the verb or adjective. • Verb to noun: increase (verb) becomes an increase (noun); grow becomes growth; decide becomes a decision. • Adjective to noun: important becomes importance; poor becomes poverty; scarce becomes scarcity. Once you have the noun, you rebuild the sentence around it, usually with a light verb such as be, occur, lead to, or result in, and a linking preposition such as in or of. Verb-based: The population increased rapidly. Noun-based: There was a rapid increase in the population.
9.2 The word families you need
Build a mental store of these verb-to-noun and adjective-to-noun pairs. They recur endlessly in IELTS topics. Verb to noun

Verb Noun Verb Noun increase an increase reduce a reduction grow growth improve an improvement develop development decline a decline produce production consume consumption pollute pollution decide a decision expand expansion fail a failure migrate migration invest investment analyse analysis contribute a contribution introduce the introduction apply an application

Adjective Noun Adjective Noun important importance poor poverty available availability scarce scarcity able ability strong strength high height long length wide width difficult difficulty stable stability efficient efficiency

grow → growth, decide → a decision; important → importance, poor → poverty, scarce →

blocks.text: 9.3 How to restructure a sentence around the noun

There are three reliable moves. Move 1 · “There was / occurred” plus the noun. > The economy grew sharply. → There was a sharp growth in the economy. / A sharp growth in the economy occurred. Move 2 · Make the noun the subject, and use a cause-and-effect verb. This is the densest, most academic version. > Because the population grew, housing became scarce. → Population growth led to housing scarcity. > Cities expanded, so traffic worsened. → Urban expansion resulted in worsening traffic. Move 3 · Adjective to “the X of” phrase. > Education is important. → the importance of education > Clean water is necessary for health. → the necessity of clean water for health Notice what happens to the sentence in Move 2: two clauses joined by because collapse into one tight noun-based clause. “Because the population grew, housing became scarce” (a full complex sentence) becomes “Population growth led to housing scarcity” (denser, more formal, fewer words). That compression is exactly what examiners mean by academic density.

blocks.text: 9.4 Why it reads as academic, and the paraphrasing payoff

Compare the two versions once more: “Because the population grew, housing became scarce.” (clause-heavy, conversational) “Population growth led to housing scarcity.” (noun-heavy, formal) The second is denser (more meaning in fewer words), more objective (it states a relationship between two things rather than telling a small story), and it sits in exactly the register Task 2

rewards. Build the habit of asking, whenever you write an action: is there a noun form of this verb, and would the sentence be tighter built around it? The Task 1 paraphrasing payoff. Nominalisation is the fastest way to reword a prompt without repeating it. When the prompt says “the number of cars increased,” you can write “there was a rise in the number of cars,” or “an increase in car ownership was recorded.” Because copying the prompt’s words costs you marks, this reworking is a direct, reliable gain.

Common Pitfall · Do not nominalise everything Nominalisation is a seasoning, not the whole meal. Two dangers: 1. Overuse makes writing heavy and lifeless. A paragraph in which every verb has become a noun is hard to read and sounds bureaucratic. Keep a mix: some strong verbs, some nominalised phrases. 2. It can bury the doer. “A decision was reached” hides who decided. Sometimes that is useful (objectivity); sometimes your argument needs to name the actor, and a plain verb is clearer. Use nominalisation for topic sentences, Task 1 openings, and cause-and-effect statements, and let ordinary verbs carry the rest.

Chapter 10 · Full Essay Editing & Proofreading Drills

The strongest candidates do not proofread by vague rereading. They proofread by category: one focused pass hunting only for one type of error, then another pass for the next type. This turns proofreading into a checklist you can actually finish in the two or three minutes you have at the end. Give each of your recurring error types a code, and hunt one code per pass. The error-code system used in this book:

Code Error type On this pass, ask  SVA subject-verb agreement Does every verb match its  true subject?  T tense Is the timeline consistent and  correct?  A article / noun number Does every noun have the  right article and  singular/plural form?  P preposition Are time, place, data, and  dependent prepositions

Code Error type On this pass, ask  correct?  WF word form Adjective vs adverb, verb vs  noun, double comparatives  C clause / punctuation Fragments, run-ons, comma  splices, missing commas  WW wrong word / collocation Direct-translation errors,  wrong linker, wrong choice  COND conditional Are the two halves matched?  No “will/would” after “if”
For most Bangladeshi candidates, two or three codes account for the majority of lost marks, usually A (articles) and SVA (the missing -s). Learn which codes catch you most, and drill those first.
How to use these drills

Each drill gives you a Band 5.5 essay with errors hidden throughout. Do this:  1. Read it once for meaning.  2. Run a separate pass for each code above, marking every error you find.  3. Rewrite the whole essay correctly with a pen.  4. Only then compare with the corrected version and the coded breakdown in the answer  key. Do not read the key first. The whole point is to train your own eye.

Chapter 10 · Part 2 · Speaking Transcript Polish

Written editing and spoken upgrading are not the same skill. In Speaking, the goal is not to turn your answer into a formal essay. Examiners reward natural, flowing speech, so a polished Band 8 or 9 answer keeps its contractions (I’m, I’ve, don’t), its discourse markers (to be honest, that said, I suppose, actually), and its relaxed rhythm. What changes is the grammar underneath: the errors are removed, and a wider range of structures (relative clauses, the present perfect, conditionals, hedging) is folded in so naturally that it still sounds like a person talking, not reciting. Remember one thing from the scoring blueprint: in Speaking, self-correction is allowed and even rewarded. If you say a wrong form and immediately fix it, that shows control. The models below show the finished, fluent version; in the real test, a small self-correction on the way there is perfectly fine. অধ্যায় ১০ পার্ট ২-এর মূল কথা: speaking-এ উত্তরকে রচনার মতো আনুষ্ঠানিক করা লক্ষ্য নয়। ব্যান্ড ৮-৯ উত্তরেও contraction, discourse marker ও স্বাভাবিক ছন্দ থাকে; শুধু নিচের grammar ঠিক হয় এবং বেশি বৈচিত্র্যময় গঠন স্বাভাবিকভাবে যোগ হয়। speaking-এ নিজে ভু ল শুধরে নেওয়া (self-correction) ভালো লক্ষণ।
Transcript 1 · Speaking Part 1 (Your hometown)

Band 6.0 version: > “I am coming from a small town near Dhaka. It is called Manikganj. I live there since my childhood. The people there is very friendly and the environment is peaceful. There is not much facility like big city, but I am liking it because it is quiet. Nowadays many young people is leaving the town for job, so it is becoming empty little bit.” Band 8/9 version (natural and correct): > “I’m from a small town near Dhaka called Manikganj, and I’ve actually lived there my whole life. The people are really friendly and the whole place has a lovely, peaceful feel to it. There aren’t as many facilities as you’d find in a big city, but to be honest that’s part of why I like it, it’s nice and quiet. That said, a lot of young people have been leaving recently to look for work, so it has started to feel a bit emptier than it used to.” What changed: I am coming from to I’m from (T, no continuous); I live there since to I’ve lived there (T, present perfect with “since”); the people there is to the people are (SVA); I am liking it to I like it (T, stative); many young people is leaving to have been leaving (SVA + T, present perfect continuous). Range added: a relative reduction (“called Manikganj”), an “as … as” comparison, the present perfect, and natural markers (“to be honest,” “that said”). BN: stative verb (like) continuous নয়, since + present perfect, আর SVA ঠিক করা হয়েছে; সেই সঙ্গে relative ও present perfect যোগ করে স্বাভাবিক রেখে উন্নত করা হয়েছে।

Transcript 4 · Speaking Part 3 (Technology and society)

Band 6.0 version: > “Yes, I think technology change our life a lot. In past, people was communicating by letter, but now everything is instant. It has many advantage, for example we can talk with anyone anytime. But there is also disadvantage. Many people is becoming addicted to phone and they don’t spend time with family. If government will make some rules, maybe it can control. In future, I think technology will become more powerful and we cannot live without it.” Band 8/9 version: > “Yes, I’d say technology has changed our lives dramatically. In the past, people used to communicate by letter, whereas now everything is more or less instant. It obviously has huge advantages, in the sense that we can reach almost anyone at any time. That said, there are downsides too. A lot of people are becoming addicted to their phones, and as a result they end up neglecting their families. I suppose if governments introduced some sensible

regulations, that might help to keep it under control. Looking ahead, I think technology will only become more powerful, to the point where we probably won’t be able to live without it.” What changed: technology change our life to has changed our lives (T + SVA + A/number); In past to In the past (A); people was communicating to used to communicate (SVA + T); many advantage to huge advantages (A/number); there is also disadvantage to there are downsides too (SVA + A/number); many people is becoming to a lot of people are becoming (SVA); they don’t spend time with family to they end up neglecting their families (collocation + A/number); If government will make some rules, maybe it can control to if governments introduced some sensible regulations, that might help to keep it under control (COND, second conditional + hedging). Range added: a “whereas” contrast clause, a second conditional, hedging (“I suppose,” “might,” “probably”), and a result structure (“to the point where”). BN: present perfect, used to, second conditional ও hedging যোগ করে উন্নত করা হয়েছে; In past→In the past article ঠিক।
Transcript 5 · Speaking Part 3 (Investing in education)

Band 6.0 version: > “I strongly believe education is most important thing for a country. If a country have educated people, it will develop fast. In my country, many poor student cannot continue study because of money. So I think government should give more scholarship. Some people says free education is waste of money, but I am not agree. When people is educated, they get good job and they pay tax, so the money come back. That is why investing in education is always good decision.” Band 8/9 version: > “I strongly believe that education is one of the most important things for any country. If a country has a well-educated population, it tends to develop far more quickly. The problem, at least where I’m from, is that a lot of students from poorer backgrounds have to drop out simply because they can’t afford it, which is why I think the government should offer far more scholarships. Some people argue that free education is a waste of money, but I don’t really agree with that. Once people are educated, they tend to find better jobs and pay more tax, so in a sense the money comes back to the state. That’s exactly why investing in education is nearly always a sound decision.” What changed: most important thing to one of the most important things (A/number + hedge); If a country have … it will develop fast to if a country has … it tends to develop far more quickly (SVA + hedge + WF adverb + grading); many poor student cannot continue study to a lot of students from poorer backgrounds have to drop out (A/number + collocation); government should give more scholarship to which is why … should offer far more scholarships (A/number + relative clause); some people says to argue (SVA); is waste of money to is a waste of money (A); I am not agree to I don’t really agree (grammar of “agree”); When people is educated to Once people are educated (SVA + subordinator); the money come back to the money comes back (SVA); That is why … always good decision to That’s exactly why … nearly always a sound decision (A + hedge). Range added: “one of the most,” a first conditional, “tends to,” a relative clause, and hedging throughout.

clause, tends to ও hedging যোগ করে ব্যান্ড ৮-৯ করা হয়েছে, তবে ভাষা স্বাভাবিক ও কথ্য রাখা হয়েছে।

blocks.text: The takeaway for Speaking Notice what the Band 8/9 versions do not do: they do not become stiff, they do not remove every contraction, and they do not sound memorised. They fix the grammar and quietly widen the range, while keeping the warmth and flow of real speech. That combination, accuracy plus natural range, is exactly what the Speaking band descriptor for Grammatical Range and Accuracy is describing. BN: ব্যান্ড ৮-৯ speaking মানে ভু লহীন ও বৈচিত্র্যময় grammar, কিন্তু ভাষা স্বাভাবিক, কথ্য ও প্রাণবন্ত থাকবে, মুখস্থ বা কাঠখোট্টা নয়।
